title: BEM: Learning Bregman Divergences forConcept Erasure in Flow Matching Models

paper.title: BEM: Learning Bregman Divergences for Concept Erasure in Flow Matching Models
paper.abstract:
Abstract Concept erasure removes harmful, private, or copyrighted concepts from text-to-image models while preserving their
other abilities. Leading models such as FLUX and Stable Diffusion 3 are trained with flow matching, and erasure
methods for them fine-tune the model toward a guided teacher’s velocities under a Euclidean loss. Yet the squared
distance is only one member of a larger family: Bregman divergences are exactly the losses under which flow matching
recovers the correct velocity field, and each member shapes differently what is erased and what is preserved. We
introduce BEM (Bregman erasure matching), which is, to our knowledge, the first to learn this divergence through bi-level optimization, so that the fine-tuned
model forgets the concept on unseen prompts while its unrelated generations stay unchanged. In the experiments we
target the suppression of nudity, violence, real identities, and copyrighted characters. Under the evaluation protocol of GEM, BEM removes more of the
concept than GEM on most settings, cutting the unsafe rate on bloody gore from 53.9 % 53.9\% to 14.4 % 14.4\% and the FID on
nudity from 8.64 8.64 to 6.64 6.64 , while retention holds on some concepts and degrades on others.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Text-to-image models based on flow matching are deployed at scale, and with them comes the problem of removing what they should not produce. A released checkpoint may reproduce nudity and graphic violence, the likeness of real people, and the style of copyrighted characters, all of which the operator of a service may be required to remove ( Schramowski et al., 2023 ; Huang et al., 2024 ) . Retraining on a filtered corpus costs as much as the original training run. The concept is therefore removed after the fact, by fine-tuning the model against itself, and this is the setting we consider. Erasure by velocity matching. Recent work shares one construction, built from two copies of the model. At each latent a frozen teacher supplies a velocity for a prompt naming the concept ( 𝒖 c {\bm{u}}_{c} ) and a velocity for an anchor prompt describing what should appear instead ( 𝒖 a {\bm{u}}_{a} ). A target velocity is formed by extrapolating away from the concept, 𝒖 ¯ = 𝒖 a + s ⁡ ( 𝒖 a − 𝒖 c ) \bar{{\bm{u}}}={\bm{u}}_{a}+s\,({\bm{u}}_{a}-{\bm{u}}_{c}) , and a student (in practice a low-rank adapter) is fit to it on partially denoised latents. The construction goes back to ESD by Gandikota et al. (2023) and carries over to the rectified flow transformers that the current models use ( Gao et al., 2025a ; Fan et al., 2026 ; Grebe et al., 2026 ) . These methods differ in how 𝒖 ¯ \bar{{\bm{u}}} is built, i.e., in the anchor, the noise levels at which the regression is applied, and the reach s s of the extrapolation, where s = 0 s=0 regresses onto the anchor itself, as CA ( Kumari et al., 2023 ) does. The unexamined component. Where these methods regress, they use the squared distance as error, which is oblivious to the direction in the velocity space. A concept, however, occupies a direction, namely the one along which the teacher separates the concept prompt from the anchor. Charging the orthogonal directions alike is what makes an erasure procedure trade the concept against everything else the model can draw, and the literature reports the consequence as a degradation of image fidelity ( Gandikota et al., 2023 ; Grebe et al., 2026 ) . Note that not every loss is admissible here. A regression of this form is a flow matching regression, and the losses under which such a regression recovers its target are known to be exactly the Bregman divergences (Theorem 2.1 below). Thus the squared distance is only one choice within a family (the choice generated by the quadratic potential φ ⁡ ( 𝒗 ) = ∥ 𝒗 ∥ 2 \varphi({\bm{v}})=\lVert{\bm{v}}\rVert^{2} ), and no erasure method varies this choice. This work. In this paper we keep the unlearning procedure of Grebe et al. (2026) unchanged, i.e., its LoRA ( Hu et al., 2022 ) adapter, its frozen teacher, its window of noise levels and its optimizer, except in two respects: we replace its hinge loss by a regression under a Bregman divergence, which is generated by a strictly convex potential φ \varphi , and we add meta steps that learn φ \varphi . Intuitively, this means that the unlearning procedure is told what a velocity error costs along the direction that carries the concept, separately from what it costs along the directions that carry everything else, instead of being told that errors in all directions cost the same. The potential is learned through bi-level optimization: the inner problem erases the concept under the Bregman divergence generated by the current potential, and the outer problem minimizes a scoring function of the resulting model, so that the potential is chosen by how well its divergence erases the concept and retains everything else rather than by how well the erasure fits. Contributions. This paper takes a known characterization of the valid losses for flow matching, observes that all erasure methods that regress make a single choice within it, and learns this choice instead of fixing it: • We observe that erasure by velocity matching inherits the valid family of flow matching (Theorem 2.1 ), so that the divergence is a free parameter of every such method. Prior work sets it to the squared distance and does not vary it. • We propose BEM, which parameterizes the potential as a bounded, context-dependent metric with a separate curvature along the direction that separates the concept from the anchor, and learns it by bi-level optimization with an implicit-function-theorem hypergradient. • On six concepts and two model families we compare against the protocol with its other components held fixed, so that a difference is attributable to the loss, not to the many other choices that an erasure procedure involves. • BEM erases more of the concept than GEM ( Grebe et al., 2026 ) , whose loss it replaces, on every concept we evaluate. On nudity it is better on five of the six benchmarks, on bloody gore it leaves 14.4 % 14.4\% unsafe against 53.9 % 53.9\% , at a lower FID in both, on the four rights-protected concepts it leaves at most 1 % 1\% against up to 10 % 10\% , and on Stable Diffusion 3.5 it leaves 3 % 3\% against 17 % 17\% . Retention rises on two of these concepts, holds on one, and falls on two.

sections.heading: 2 Background
sections.text: The models this paper edits, FLUX ( Black Forest Labs et al., 2025 ) and Stable Diffusion 3 ( Esser et al., 2024 ) , are trained by flow matching. This section recalls its objective, introduces Bregman divergences, and states the result that ties the two together.

sections.heading: 2.1 Flow Matching
sections.text: A flow matching model generates an image by integrating an ordinary differential equation from a Gaussian sample 𝒙 0 {\bm{x}}_{0} , d d ​ t ​ 𝒙 t = 𝒗 𝜽 ​ ( 𝒙 t , t , c ) , t : 0 → 1 , \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\,{\bm{x}}_{t}\;=\;{\bm{v}}_{{\bm{\theta}}}({\bm{x}}_{t},t,c),\qquad t:0\to 1, (1) where 𝒙 t ∈ ℝ d {\bm{x}}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} is the latent at time t t , c c is the text prompt, 𝒗 𝜽 {\bm{v}}_{{\bm{\theta}}} is a neural network with parameters 𝜽 {\bm{\theta}} , and the image is 𝒙 1 {\bm{x}}_{1} . FLUX and Stable Diffusion 3 parameterize time so that t = 0 t=0 is data and t = 1 t=1 is noise; this flips the sign of the velocity and changes nothing below. Flow matching fixes the interpolation between noise and data by hand ( Lipman et al., 2022 ; Liu et al., 2022 ) : one draws a pair 𝒛 {\bm{z}} of noise and data from a coupling and interpolates between the two, along the straight line for the rectified flows of the models above. The interpolant determines a conditional velocity 𝒖 t ​ ( 𝒙 ∣ 𝒛 ) {\bm{u}}_{t}({\bm{x}}\mid{\bm{z}}) in closed form, but what generates the data is its average over all pairs that pass through the same latent, 𝒖 t ​ ( 𝒙 ) = 𝔼 ⁡ [ 𝒖 t ​ ( 𝒙 ∣ 𝒛 ) | 𝒙 t = 𝒙 ] , {\bm{u}}_{t}({\bm{x}})\;=\;\mathbb{E}\big[\,{\bm{u}}_{t}({\bm{x}}\mid{\bm{z}})\;\big|\;{\bm{x}}_{t}={\bm{x}}\,\big], (2) the marginal field. Training is possible because the two have the same gradient ( Lipman et al., 2022 ; Lipman et al., 2024 ) , ∇ 𝜽 ℒ FM ​ ( 𝜽 ) = ∇ 𝜽 ℒ CFM ​ ( 𝜽 ) , \nabla_{{\bm{\theta}}}\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FM}}({\bm{\theta}})\;=\;\nabla_{{\bm{\theta}}}\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CFM}}({\bm{\theta}}), (4) and nothing so far requires the squared distance itself.

sections.heading: 2.2 Bregman Divergences
sections.text: Let φ : ℝ d → ℝ \varphi:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R} be strictly convex and continuously differentiable. The Bregman divergence generated by φ \varphi ( Bregman, 1967 ) is the gap at 𝒖 {\bm{u}} between φ \varphi and its linearization at 𝒗 {\bm{v}} , D φ ​ ( 𝒖 , 𝒗 ) = φ ⁡ ( 𝒖 ) − φ ⁡ ( 𝒗 ) − ⟨ ∇ φ ​ ( 𝒗 ) , 𝒖 − 𝒗 ⟩ . D_{\varphi}({\bm{u}},{\bm{v}})\;=\;\varphi({\bm{u}})-\varphi({\bm{v}})-\langle\nabla\varphi({\bm{v}}),\,{\bm{u}}-{\bm{v}}\rangle. (5) It is nonnegative, vanishes exactly at 𝒖 = 𝒗 {\bm{u}}={\bm{v}} , and is in general not symmetric. Two choices of φ \varphi are familiar: φ ⁡ ( 𝒗 ) = ∥ 𝒗 ∥ 2 \varphi({\bm{v}})=\lVert{\bm{v}}\rVert^{2} gives the squared distance ∥ 𝒖 − 𝒗 ∥ 2 \lVert{\bm{u}}-{\bm{v}}\rVert^{2} , and the negative entropy gives the Kullback-Leibler divergence. Intuitively, φ \varphi fixes how the cost of an error grows with its direction and magnitude, and the squared distance is the choice that makes the cost the same in every direction.

sections.heading: 2.3 The Valid Losses for Flow Matching
sections.text: The two meet in a known result. Replace the squared distance in Eq. Let D : ℝ d × ℝ d → ℝ ≥ 0 D:\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} be smooth with D ⁡ ( 𝐮 , 𝐯 ) = 0 D({\bm{u}},{\bm{v}})=0 if and only if 𝐮 = 𝐯 {\bm{u}}={\bm{v}} . Then ∇ 𝜽 ℒ FM D ( 𝜽 ) = ∇ 𝜽 ℒ CFM D ( 𝜽 ) for all 𝜽 ⟺ D = D φ for a strictly convex φ . \nabla_{{\bm{\theta}}}\,\mathcal{L}^{D}_{\mathrm{FM}}({\bm{\theta}})\;=\;\nabla_{{\bm{\theta}}}\,\mathcal{L}^{D}_{\mathrm{CFM}}({\bm{\theta}})\quad\text{for all }{\bm{\theta}}\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad D=D_{\varphi}\ \text{ for a strictly convex }\varphi. The forward direction is the standard conditional flow matching argument and is proved by Lipman et al. (2024) , Section 4.5. The converse is the part that matters here, since it says that no loss outside the family Eq. ( 5 ) admits tractable training in this sense; it is proved by Holderrieth et al. Thus the choice made by every erasure method, the squared distance, is a single choice within a family that is fixed by nothing but convention, and moving inside that family leaves training as tractable as it was.

sections.heading: 3 Related Work
sections.text: We review erasure in diffusion models, attacks on erased models and defenses against them, erasure in flow models, and the unlearning procedure of GEM on which we build. Tab. 10 in App. D lists these methods with the models they are evaluated on and what they minimize, and Kim & Qi (2025) survey the field more broadly. Erasure in diffusion models. Methods for diffusion models edit the weights in closed form, fine-tune them or act at sampling time. Closed-form methods edit the cross-attention or the text encoder ( Orgad et al., 2023 ; Arad et al., 2024 ; Gandikota et al., 2024 ; Gong et al., 2024 ; Lu et al., 2024 ) . Among fine-tuning methods, ESD ( Gandikota et al., 2023 ) introduced the teacher-guided regression of Sec. 1 , with the empty prompt as anchor. CA ( Kumari et al., 2023 ) and others ( Kim et al., 2023 ; Lyu et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2025 ; Bui et al., 2024 ) change its target or what it preserves. Further methods alter the training signal or the fine-tuned component ( Ni et al., 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2024a ; Poppi et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2024 ) , or adapt machine unlearning ( Heng & Soh, 2023 ; Fan et al., 2024 ; Wu & Harandi, 2024 ) . DUO ( Park et al., 2024 ) optimizes preferences, EraseFlow ( Kusumba et al., 2025 ) a trajectory-balance criterion, and EraseDiff ( Wu et al., 2025 ) a bi-level problem. Note that where the methods above regress, they use the squared distance. Sampling-time methods leave the weights unchanged. They rewrite the prompt ( Ni et al., 2024 ) , change the guidance ( Schramowski et al., 2023 ; Jain et al., 2024 ) , project the text embeddings off an unsafe subspace ( Yoon et al., 2025 ) or add learned concept directions to the activations ( Li et al., 2024 ) . Robustness. Several attacks recover erased concepts. Ring-A-Bell ( Tsai et al., 2024 ) , P4D ( Chin et al., 2024 ) and UnlearnDiff ( Zhang et al., 2024c ) optimize the prompt. Pham et al. (2024) learn token embeddings instead, and ReFlux ( Jiang et al., 2025 ) reactivates erased concepts in FLUX. MMA-Diffusion ( Yang et al., 2024 ) bypasses prompt filters and safety checkers. Defenses train against such attacks ( Huang et al., 2024 ; Kim et al., 2024 ; Srivatsan et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2024b ) or resist fine-tuning back toward the concept ( Zheng & Yeh, 2024 ; Gao et al., 2025b ) . We evaluate on the prompts of Ring-A-Bell, MMA-Diffusion and P4D but do not train against attacks. Flow models. EraseAnything ( Gao et al., 2025a ) carries the teacher-guided construction to rectified flow transformers. It places erasure and preservation in the two levels of a bi-level problem, which EraseAnything++ ( Fan et al., 2026 ) recasts as a constrained multi-objective problem. Other methods handle single-stream transformers ( Jiang et al., 2026 ) , regress the final outputs of the sampler through all steps ( Zhang et al., 2025b ) , optimize erasure and preservation rewards ( Sun et al., 2026a ) or unlearn by flow matching toward a reweighted target ( Simone et al., 2025 ) . Without training, DVE ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) projects the velocity off the direction in which the concept and anchor velocities differ, and Mosaic ( Ko et al., 2026 ) blends the velocity fields of erased models per region. The unlearning procedure we build on. GEM ( Grebe et al., 2026 ) bridges the trajectory view of EraseFlow and the teacher-guided view of ESD. From the trajectory view it takes one observation: erasure should be reinforced across a segment of the generation path, not at one noise level. It therefore fixes a window, the first t stop + 1 t_{\mathrm{stop}}+1 steps of the sampler counted from the noise, and evaluates all the velocities in it in parallel. From the teacher-guided view it takes the frozen teacher, which supplies a safe and an unsafe velocity. Its objective, however, is not a regression. Write d positive d_{\mathrm{positive}} for the distance of the student to the teacher’s velocity on the anchor prompt, and d negative d_{\mathrm{negative}} for its distance to the teacher’s velocity on the concept prompt. GEM minimizes the contrastive hinge ℒ GEM ​ ( 𝜽 ) = max ⁡ ( 0 , d positive − η ​ d negative ) , \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{GEM}}({\bm{\theta}})\;=\;\max\big(0,\;d_{\mathrm{positive}}-\eta\,d_{\mathrm{negative}}\big), (7) which pulls the student toward the safe velocity and pushes it away from the unsafe one. A noise level switches off once d positive ≤ η ​ d negative d_{\mathrm{positive}}\leq\eta\,d_{\mathrm{negative}} . In contrast to these methods, BEM learns the loss. EraseAnything and EraseDiff optimize the model at both levels of their bi-level problems, DVE removes the concept direction at sampling time and GEM minimizes a hinge. The outer level of our bi-level problem instead learns the potential that defines the loss, which weights the concept direction inside a regression. We build on GEM for three reasons. First, it is a recent state-of-the-art method: among the methods it compares with, it reports the lowest unsafe rates on all nudity and gore benchmarks we use (App. A.2 ). Second, its objective is a single loss on the velocities, so the loss is what defines the method, whereas other methods for flow models add further terms, such as attention terms or constraints. GEM is therefore the natural setting in which to study the loss itself. Third, its released code reproduces the reported results closely on most benchmarks (App. A.2 ), which we did not find for all the methods we considered. We therefore keep its unlearning procedure and swap the hinge loss of Eq. ( 7 ) for a learned Bregman divergence.

sections.heading: 4 Learning the Divergence
sections.text: We adopt the unlearning procedure of GEM ( Grebe et al., 2026 ) , i.e., its low-rank adapter on the attention projections of the frozen base model, its frozen teacher, its window of noise levels, its partially denoised latents and its optimizer, and replace the hinge loss of Eq. ( 7 ) by a regression under a Bregman divergence. From here on 𝜽 {\bm{\theta}} denotes the parameters of the adapter and 𝒗 𝜽 {\bm{v}}_{{\bm{\theta}}} the velocity of the adapted model, the student. The teacher is queried twice at the same latent: we write 𝒖 c {\bm{u}}_{c} for its velocity on a prompt that names the concept, 𝒖 a {\bm{u}}_{a} for its velocity on an anchor prompt that describes what should appear instead, and Δ = 𝒖 a − 𝒖 c \Delta={\bm{u}}_{a}-{\bm{u}}_{c} for the separation of the two. For a strictly convex potential φ \varphi , unlearning minimizes ℒ BEM ​ ( 𝜽 , φ ) = D φ ​ ( 𝒖 ¯ , 𝒗 𝜽 ) , 𝒖 ¯ = 𝒖 a + s ​ Δ , \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{BEM}}({\bm{\theta}};\varphi)\;=\;D_{\varphi}\big(\bar{{\bm{u}}},\,{\bm{v}}_{{\bm{\theta}}}\big),\qquad\bar{{\bm{u}}}\;=\;{\bm{u}}_{a}+s\,\Delta, (8) where D φ D_{\varphi} is the Bregman divergence of Eq. ( 5 ) and the student is queried on the concept prompt at the same latent as the teacher. The target 𝒖 ¯ \bar{{\bm{u}}} is the anchor velocity extrapolated away from the concept by the reach s ≥ 0 s\geq 0 . By Theorem 2.1 , every D φ D_{\varphi} is a valid flow matching loss, and φ ⁡ ( 𝒗 ) = ∥ 𝒗 ∥ 2 \varphi({\bm{v}})=\lVert{\bm{v}}\rVert^{2} gives the squared distance of the regressions in Sec. 3 . Thus choosing the loss amounts to choosing φ \varphi . In the rest of this section we state how a potential is judged (Sec. 4.1 ), construct a family of potentials (Sec. 4.2 ), and select a potential from it by bi-level optimization (Sec. 4.3 ).

sections.heading: 4.1 Judging a Potential
sections.text: We now ask how to learn φ \varphi . Note that Eq. ( 8 ) cannot judge its own potential: zero loss means that the student matches 𝒖 ¯ \bar{{\bm{u}}} where it was trained, and says nothing about how well it erases the concept or retains everything else. We therefore judge a potential by the model that results from unlearning with it. A good potential yields a student that erases the concept and retains everything else, and we measure both with the meta loss ℒ meta ​ ( 𝜽 ) = ℒ erasure ​ ( 𝜽 ) + ρ ​ ℒ retention ​ ( 𝜽 ) , \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{meta}}({\bm{\theta}})\;=\;\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{erasure}}({\bm{\theta}})\;+\;\rho\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{retention}}({\bm{\theta}}), (9) evaluated at the adapter after unlearning. The weight ρ \rho balances the erasure criterion ℒ erasure \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{erasure}} and the retention criterion ℒ retention \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{retention}} ; we hold ρ = 0.05 \rho=0.05 on nudity and set it by the rule of App. C.2 elsewhere. Theorem 2.1 does not constrain Eq. ( 9 ): the theorem governs a loss that trains a velocity field, and Eq. ( 9 ) only scores one that is already trained. We detail the two criteria next. Erasure criterion. Let 𝒗 {\bm{v}} be the velocity of the student on the concept prompt (computed at its latent) and Δ \Delta the separation of the concept prompt from its anchor at that latent. We want to know how far the student has traveled from the concept toward the anchor, so we project its displacement onto Δ \Delta , κ i = ⟨ 𝒗 i − 𝒖 c , i , Δ i ⟩ ∥ Δ i ∥ 2 , \kappa_{i}\;=\;\frac{\langle{\bm{v}}_{i}-{\bm{u}}_{c,i},\,\Delta_{i}\rangle}{\lVert\Delta_{i}\rVert^{2}}, (10) where i i indexes the tokens of the latent. The projection is 0 0 at an unchanged token and 1 1 at one that has reached the anchor. Dividing by ∥ Δ i ∥ 2 \lVert\Delta_{i}\rVert^{2} makes κ i \kappa_{i} scale free, and κ i \kappa_{i} ignores motion orthogonal to Δ i \Delta_{i} . The erasure criterion is ℒ erasure ​ ( 𝜽 ) = ∑ i m i ​ σ ​ ( 1 − κ i ) , m i = ∥ Δ i ∥ 2 / ∑ j ∥ Δ j ∥ 2 , \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{erasure}}({\bm{\theta}})\;=\;\textstyle\sum_{i}m_{i}\,\sigma\big(1-\kappa_{i}\big),\qquad m_{i}\;=\;\lVert\Delta_{i}\rVert^{2}\Big/\textstyle\sum_{j}\lVert\Delta_{j}\rVert^{2}, (11) averaged over a batch of fresh latents, with σ ⁡ ( x ) = softplus ⁡ ( β ​ x ) / β \sigma(x)=\mathrm{softplus}(\beta x)/\beta a smoothed hinge (we use β = 4 \beta=4 ). The saliency weights m i m_{i} concentrate the criterion on the tokens that carry the concept; where ∥ Δ i ∥ \lVert\Delta_{i}\rVert is small, the teacher barely distinguishes the two prompts and there is nothing to erase. The hinge saturates beyond κ i = 1 \kappa_{i}=1 , so that a token need do little more than reach the anchor. Retention criterion. The anchor prompt does not name the concept, so on it we want to preserve the teacher’s velocity 𝒖 a {\bm{u}}_{a} , and any deviation of the student’s velocity 𝒗 {\bm{v}} on the anchor prompt from 𝒖 a {\bm{u}}_{a} is damage. Here no direction is privileged, and the plain squared distance is the right measurement. The retention criterion is ℒ retention ​ ( 𝜽 ) = 1 U ¯ ​ ∥ 𝒗 − 𝒖 a ∥ 2 , \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{retention}}({\bm{\theta}})\;=\;\frac{1}{\bar{U}}\,\lVert{\bm{v}}-{\bm{u}}_{a}\rVert^{2}, (12) where U ¯ \bar{U} is the mean of ∥ Δ ∥ 2 \lVert\Delta\rVert^{2} over the erasure latents, so that both criteria are dimensionless.

sections.heading: 4.2 A Family of Potentials
sections.text: Concept direction. We now ask which potentials can score well on Eq. ( 9 ). The squared distance penalizes an error of a given length the same in every direction. The meta loss, however, singles out one direction: Eq. ( 10 ) scores motion along Δ \Delta only, and retention charges every direction alike. Motion along Δ \Delta is erasure, since the target 𝒖 ¯ \bar{{\bm{u}}} lies on that line. Motion orthogonal to Δ \Delta changes the velocity without removing the concept; it does not help erasure and, to the extent that it transfers to nearby prompts, harms retention. When the adapter cannot fit the target exactly, as an adapter of low rank trained for a few steps cannot, a potential that penalizes the two directions differently can therefore increase erasure at a fixed amount of damage. This is the freedom we exploit. We construct a family of potentials φ 𝝍 \varphi_{{\bm{\psi}}} , indexed by the parameters 𝝍 {\bm{\psi}} of a neural network, with three properties: (i) every 𝝍 {\bm{\psi}} yields a strictly convex potential; (ii) the family contains the squared distance; (iii) the Hessian of every member is cheap to compute. Property (iii) matters because the hypergradient in Sec. 4.3 applies the Hessian once per conjugate gradient iteration. A potential acts on the velocities of all tokens of a latent at one noise level. Architecture. We follow the partially input convex networks of Amos et al. (2017) and let the tokens interact by attention. sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We presented a new perspective on concept erasure by velocity matching. Its objective is a flow matching loss, so by Theorem 2.1 the loss may be any Bregman divergence, and the squared distance of prior regressions is one choice within that family; we made the choice a learning problem. BEM parameterizes the potential so that errors along the direction that separates the concept from its anchor can be charged differently from errors across it, and selects the potential by a bi-level problem whose meta loss scores the resulting student on erasure and retention. With the unlearning procedure of GEM ( Grebe et al., 2026 ) kept and only its loss replaced, BEM erases more of the concept on most benchmarks and on both model families, at a lower FID where we measured it, while retention holds on some concepts and falls on others. The divergence is thus a free parameter of these methods, and one that repays being learned.

sections.heading: AI use statement
sections.text: In this work, we have not used generative AI tools to develop the theoretical framework or to formulate the mathematical claims. We used generative AI tools to write boilerplate code for training and for formatting and analyzing logs, to help with debugging, to compile the overview of related methods in Tab. 10 and the tables of hyperparameters and statistics (Tabs. 9 and 8 ), to polish the writing and to format the references. We have reviewed all AI-assisted work, and we take responsibility for the final content of this work, including text, claims or artifacts produced with the aid of generative AI.

sections.heading: Ethics statement
sections.text: Concept erasure is a safety measure, and this work aims to make it more reliable. Its experiments nevertheless require the models to produce the content that erasure removes. Following the evaluation protocol of Grebe et al. (2026) , we generate images from public benchmark prompts for nudity and graphic violence (I2P, T2I-RiskyPrompts, Ring-A-Bell, MMA-Diffusion and P4D) and for the likeness of public figures and copyrighted characters. These images serve only for evaluation: automatic classifiers score them (NudeNet, Q16 and Qwen2.5-VL), and no human subjects or annotators were involved. The figures show generated gore and generated likenesses of public figures in order to document erasure and retention; nudity is censored. Two limitations matter for deployment. First, erasure by fine-tuning is not a guarantee: adversarial prompts and further fine-tuning can recover erased concepts (Sec. 3 ), and we evaluate on published attack prompts but not against attacks adapted to our models, so an erased model should not be the only safeguard. Second, erasure can damage unrelated content: on Albert Einstein, BEM retains the neighboring identities in 72.7 % 72.7\% of generations against 93.3 % 93.3\% for GEM (Sec. 5 ). Our evaluation relies on automatic classifiers, which have their own errors and biases, and App. A.2 shows how the choice of the identity classifier changes the rates. Erasure could also be used to suppress legitimate content; the method does not decide what is erased. The pretrained models and the benchmarks are used under their respective licenses for research.
